summary: Learners aged 7–9 explore the story of Pompeii and Mount Vesuvius: an ordinary Roman city buried by the AD 79 eruption, preserved under volcanic ash, and later excavated by archaeologists. The central insight is the preservation paradox — the same rapid ash burial that destroyed the city also sealed and 'froze' it, which is why a 2,000-year-old town survives as a snapshot of Roman daily life. Activities centre on in-role dialogue (eyewitness and archaeologist), then/now image exploration, event sequencing, a hands-on burial-and-excavation model, and an optional 3D reconstruction. Key factual corrections to carry throughout: Pompeii was buried by ash, pumice and hot ash surges (not a lava flow), and the famous 'bodies' are plaster casts poured into hollows left where bodies decayed in the hardened ash — not petrified real bodies. Human loss is handled sensitively and non-graphically.
misconceptions: Pompeii was destroyed by flowing lava (it was buried by ash, pumice and hot ash surges — not a lava flow).
The plaster casts are the actual preserved bodies (they are plaster poured into voids left where bodies decayed in the hardened ash).
Everyone escaped / no one was affected (many escaped, but the disaster caused real loss — handle sensitively).
Pompeii was found recently/by accident only (it was gradually rediscovered and deliberately excavated by archaeologists over centuries).
Volcanoes only destroy (here the eruption also preserved an entire city, teaching us about Roman life).

activities.title: Interview an eyewitness and an archaeologist
steps: Talk in role with Pliny the Younger, who watched Vesuvius erupt from across the bay, asking questions like 'What did you see?', 'What did it sound like?', 'Were you frightened?', 'What was the cloud shaped like?'
Switch to talking with an archaeologist excavating Pompeii and ask 'Why are there people-shaped holes in the ash?', 'How do you know how the Romans lived?', 'Why did so much survive?'
Say back, in your own words, what buried the city and why the archaeologist's answer means the casts are not real bodies
activities.insight: The eruption both destroyed Pompeii and preserved it: the ash that buried the city also sealed buildings, objects and the shapes of people, which is exactly why we can learn about Roman daily life today.

activities.title: Then-and-now Pompeii street
steps: Use a then/now view of the same Pompeii street — the buried, unexcavated state versus the excavated ruins today — sliding or tapping to compare the two states (if any reconstruction image is offered, it is clearly labelled as an artist's reconstruction, not the surviving remains)
Tap preserved features — a bakery, a cart, graffiti on a wall — to reveal what each tells us about how Romans actually lived
Tap a plaster cast to see, gently, how it was made: void in the hardened ash → plaster poured in → recovered shape
Look up to see Vesuvius looming over the bay and connect the mountain to what happened
activities.insight: A curated set of surviving everyday objects and buildings shows that a whole city was sealed in time, letting us read Roman daily life directly from what the ash preserved.

activities.title: Sequence the story and sort the clues
steps: Put the events in order: ordinary Roman Pompeii → Vesuvius erupts → city buried in ash → rediscovered → excavated by archaeologists
Answer: 'What buried Pompeii — lava or ash?' and explain the difference between a lava flow and falling/surging ash
Match preserved objects to what they tell us about Roman life (e.g. bakery → bread; cart → travel/trade; graffiti → writing)
After ordering/matching, explain in your own words how the eruption both destroyed and preserved the city
activities.insight: Consolidate the correct sequence of events and the ash-not-lava distinction, and connect specific finds to specific conclusions about Roman daily life.

activities.title: Bury it, then dig it up
steps: Watch or model ash accumulating over a small city (e.g. with a toy/model town and a dry, pourable material, or an on-screen simulation) until the buildings are covered
Carefully 'excavate' layer by layer to reveal the preserved streets and objects underneath

Describe what you observe: the covering hid the model town and also kept what was underneath in place for you to find (at the real Pompeii, many roofs fell in under the weight of the pumice, but streets, walls and many objects were kept where they were)
activities.insight: Rapid burial by ash physically seals and protects what lies beneath, so careful digging later can recover it — a concrete model of how destruction and preservation happened together.

activities.title: Walk a reconstructed Pompeii street (optional immersion extension)
steps: Explore a 3D reconstruction of a Pompeii street as it may have looked in Roman times — clearly labelled as an artist's reconstruction, not a photograph of the surviving remains
Then view the same street as excavated ruins to compare the once-living city with what actually survived
Describe one thing the reconstruction helped you picture about Roman daily life, and one thing you can only learn from the real surviving objects
activities.insight: Seeing a street first as a living Roman place and then as ruins helps connect the human city to the evidence that survived; the reconstruction is an informed interpretation, while the ruins and preserved objects are the real evidence.

checkQuestion: In the Pompeii museum you can see human body shapes. A friend says, 'Those are the actual bodies of the people, turned to stone by the volcano.' Is that right? What are those shapes really, and how did the eruption both destroy AND preserve the city?
checkAnswer: Not quite — they aren't turned-to-stone bodies. When Vesuvius erupted, ash buried Pompeii and set hard around the people; the bodies later decayed away, leaving hollow body-shaped spaces in the ash. Archaeologists poured plaster into those hollows to make the shapes we see. The eruption both destroyed the city (killed people, buried it) and preserved it (the ash sealed buildings and everyday life for centuries until it was dug up).
